topics.title: 17.2.1 Understanding public, private, and protected
topics.summary: Public members form the callable interface. Private members are implementation details available to the class and its friends. Protected members are additionally accessible in appropriate derived-class contexts. These are compile-time access-control rules, not operating-system security boundaries.

topics.summary: An invariant is a condition that must hold whenever an object is available for ordinary use. For a bounded quantity, it might be 0 <= value <= maximum. Constructors establish it, and public operations preserve it. A failed update should leave the previous valid state intact rather than partially changing the object.

topics.title: 17.3.1 Using the this Pointer
topics.summary: Inside a nonstatic member function, this points to the object on which the function was called. Member names commonly use that object implicitly. Explicit this->member can resolve naming situations or improve clarity, but it is not required before every access.

topics.summary: The public interface states what callers can ask the object to do. The private representation states how those operations are implemented. Callers that use only the interface should not need rewriting when the internal representation changes while behavior stays the same.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: Why is a Boolean return insufficient evidence? The function can return false after already changing state. Tests must inspect both the reported result and the object’s post-state.

cards.question: Why is a Boolean return insufficient evidence?
cards.answer: The function can return false after already changing state. Tests must inspect both the reported result and the object’s post-state.

cards.question: Why not store an empty flag?
cards.answer: It is derivable from the quantity. Duplicating it creates another invariant that every update must preserve.

cards.question: Why is private not a security boundary?
cards.answer: It controls ordinary source-level access within the language. It does not provide memory isolation or protect against arbitrary modification of a running process.

cards.question: Why prefer meaningful operations?
cards.answer: They expose allowed transitions and can enforce domain rules more directly than unrestricted field replacement.
